vignette: Arjun Mehta was a 41-year-old South Asian park ranger who had been in a steady relationship for several years and, until recently, had prided himself on being calm, practical, and hard to rattle. That changed after a period of captivity overseas, an experience he still described only in fragments because the full account felt too shameful and too close. What stayed with him were not stories in sequence but a set of snapshots: a metal door half open, the glare of a fluorescent light, a boot stepping into view, the hard grip on his arm, and the taste of fear in his mouth. Whenever those details were sparked by a military comment on television or the sight of uniforms at the trailhead, Arjun found himself immediately thinking that the world was not safe and that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate. After the memory broke through, he would catch himself thinking that he must now be the kind of person who could be trapped and humiliated so easily, as if the image itself proved something permanent about him. A uniform at the trailhead or a military comment on television did not just bring the memory back for Arjun; it carried an immediate verdict with it, and he would stand there thinking, with quiet certainty, that the world was unsafe and that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate for ending up in that situation. Those conclusions made the memory more vivid and easier to find, as if the snapshots waited just beneath the surface whenever he judged himself that way. When those images came back, they did so as if they were happening in the room with him; at times he could feel the old ache and pressure in the same parts of his body, and at other times he could describe the scene with a flat, numbed distance, as though it had happened to someone else. Even in the early weeks after he returned home, unexpected movement nearby made him flinch as though he were back in danger, and he could not trust reassurance. Because he had come to believe the world was unsafe and that he could not trust his own judgment, almost anything could serve as a trigger: a boot on a trail, a uniform at work, a voice raised on the television, or someone moving too quickly in his peripheral vision. Each of those moments seemed to confirm the same bleak conclusion, and the more certain he became of that conclusion, the more sensitive he was to the next cue. Friends told him he was safe; his partner said the doors were locked; Arjun still scanned the room, convinced that safety could be taken away without warning. He also began to feel permanently humiliated by what had happened, certain that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, and the humiliation deepened his sense that he was set apart from everyone around him. Once he had reached those conclusions, almost anything could become a cue: a boot on a trail, a raised voice on the television, a stranger moving too quickly in his peripheral vision, even a uniform at work could suddenly seem significant and hold his attention. That humiliation made him more alert to possible signs that it could happen again; once he had decided he could not trust his own judgment, a raised voice, a stranger turning too quickly, or a uniform in the wrong place could all snag his attention and feel like proof that danger was nearby. Those appraisals quickly shaped how he moved through the world. Arjun came to believe that being seen carried risk, so he made himself smaller in public, avoided eye contact, and went along with whatever others wanted because agreeing felt safer than being noticed. He also imposed strict control over what he ate, cutting portions and skipping meals because regulating food gave him one area where he could feel disciplined and not at the mercy of anyone else. The same avoidance that seemed to protect him also narrowed his world into a map of things he could no longer tolerate; every route he stopped taking and every interaction he shortened became another reminder that danger was still running his days. If being seen felt risky and the safest thing was to keep himself small and predictable, then agreeing too quickly, avoiding eye contact, and skipping meals were not random habits for Arjun but the only responses that seemed to make sense. The memory would come back when he was trying to keep himself controlled, and after it surfaced he would tighten those routines further, telling himself that if he could just stay disciplined enough he might keep the images at bay. But the more he skipped meals and deferred to others, the more he felt that he needed those habits, and the more his life seemed to map itself around the captivity he was trying not to think about. At the same time, he found himself replaying scenes of revenge against the people responsible, imagining power reversed and himself no longer trapped. Those scenes were not just fantasies for him; they were what he turned to when the memory broke through, a way of keeping the event in view without feeling helpless inside it. The more those scenes stayed with him, the easier the captivity became to summon in his mind, and the more likely ordinary things - a closing metal gate at work, a boot scraping gravel on a trail, a sharp tone from a radio - were to feel linked to it. Even so, each time he returned to them, the captivity felt nearer and more dangerous, and he came away thinking that he must still be deeply changed by it. Yet these efforts never settled him for long. The more he tried to control his eating, please others, or mentally punish his captors, the more the images returned in sharper pieces, each flash of the event seeming to confirm how isolated and humiliated he had become. Each time the memory came back after he had been working so hard to keep it away, it seemed to tell him that he was not really in control of anything and that something about him had been permanently altered by what had happened. That constant sense of danger was itself part of the problem: when he felt most on edge, the snapshots came back with extra force, as if his body's alarm were pulling him closer to the moment rather than away from it. On those days, the threat feeling did not stay abstract; it seemed to drag the memory forward whole, so that a sudden jolt on the trail or a burst of radio static could bring the fluorescent light, the metal door, and the grip on his arm back in one vivid rush. Feeling that threatened also made him more certain that the event had permanently altered him and that safety was something other people got, not him. The memory was especially liable to be pulled loose by military topics; if someone at home mentioned the army, or if a news report showed uniforms, his mind jumped straight back to those few terrible moments. Uniforms also set off the same reaction at work, where, as a park ranger, he sometimes encountered law enforcement or search-and-rescue personnel in similar clothing. Being seen in those moments felt exposing, and once he was self-conscious under someone's gaze, he would think again that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate, which only made the old images more vivid and shameful. As the months passed, the memory itself started to drive the rest of the cycle. Keeping the memory at bay through strict routines and silence only seemed to keep it alive; the less he spoke about it and the more tightly he managed himself, the more intact and ready to return those snapshots felt. A sudden return of the snapshot images could bring a wave of bodily pain and make him feel as if the captivity were happening again, and once that threat feeling rose he became even more certain that he could not trust safety. When he was jolted by a sound or an abrupt movement on a trail, the room or forest seemed to tilt toward the past, and that sense of danger made the fragments of memory sharper still. The memories, in turn, fed back into his negative beliefs: each return seemed to prove that he remained isolated, permanently humiliated, and somehow at fault. Because he felt that way, he redoubled his efforts to keep control, eating even more strictly, deferring to others, and fantasizing about revenge in private. But these strategies brought their own costs. Skipping meals left him shaky and more reactive to sudden movement, which made the world feel even less safe. Going along with everyone else left him resentful and more aware of being unseen. Staying in those patterns without ever testing whether he could manage differently left the original threat feeling untouched, and in his body's accounting that meant the danger must still be real. Revenge fantasies kept his mind circling the captivity long after work, making the images easier to summon and the humiliation harder to shake. And once he was already keyed up, even a uniform at the trailhead, a military comment on television, or a stranger turning too quickly on the path could trigger the same surge of dread and pull him back into the snapshots again. By the time he sought help, Arjun was still functioning at work but only by keeping himself tightly managed and on edge. His partner had noticed that he was distant at home, jumpy when someone moved unexpectedly, and increasingly unwilling to go out unless he could control the setting. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was becoming trapped in the same private loop every day: the images, the humiliation, the rigid control, the constant scanning. He said he was most afraid that the captivity had permanently changed him, but he was also hoping that therapy might help him feel safe enough to stop living as if danger were always one step away. After weeks of skipping meals and deferring to everyone else, he came to read those habits as proof that he could not manage on his own, which only deepened the humiliation and made him more certain that the event had changed him for good.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers leading to intrusive memory, but it does not clearly state that triggers directly cause his negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette states that appraisals shaped his behavior, but it does not show negative appraisals causing the memory to recur or intensify.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly show negative appraisals generating triggers or making him more trigger-sensitive.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette shows maladaptive strategies increasing memory vividness only indirectly; it does not clearly state that the memory itself leads to those strategies.
  e.g. "She had learned that if she kept the television on loud enough, the thoughts couldn't get a foothold — silence was the enemy."
  e.g. "After the memory surfaced during sex, she began finding quiet reasons to avoid intimacy altogether, telling herself she was simply tired or stressed."
  e.g. "To stop the images coming at night, she started staying up later and later, until exhaustion was the only reliable way to fall asleep."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette shows threat feelings rising from the memories, but it does not clearly state threat causing the memory to return or intensify.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows threat reinforcing safety concerns, but it does not clearly state threat producing negative appraisals.
  e.g. "The constant sense of danger was the most convincing proof she had that her life had changed beyond repair."
  e.g. "Feeling this afraid all the time, she had eventually come to accept the conclusion her body kept offering: that she was not the kind of person who got to feel safe."
  e.g. "The threat that shadowed her days quietly confirmed the thought she worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who she was now."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette describes strategies worsening safety and reactivity, but it does not clearly state the memory causing those maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies create or intensify triggers.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not clearly state that maladaptive strategies increase threat or danger feelings directly.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Arjun Mehta was a 41-year-old South Asian park ranger who had been in a steady relationship for several years and, until recently, had prided himself on being calm, practical, and hard to rattle. That changed after a period of captivity overseas, an experience he still described only in fragments because the full account felt too shameful and too close. What stayed with him were not stories in sequence but a set of snapshots: a metal door half open, the glare of a fluorescent light, a boot stepping into view, the hard grip on his arm, and the taste of fear in his mouth. Whenever those details were sparked by a military comment on television or the sight of uniforms at the trailhead, Arjun found himself immediately thinking that the world was not safe and that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate. After the memory broke through, he would catch himself thinking that he must now be the kind of person who could be trapped and humiliated so easily, as if the image itself proved something permanent about him. A uniform at the trailhead or a military comment on television did not just bring the memory back for Arjun; it carried an immediate verdict with it, and he would stand there thinking, with quiet certainty, that the world was unsafe and that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate for ending up in that situation. Those conclusions made the memory more vivid and easier to find, as if the snapshots waited just beneath the surface whenever he judged himself that way. When those images came back, they did so as if they were happening in the room with him; at times he could feel the old ache and pressure in the same parts of his body, and at other times he could describe the scene with a flat, numbed distance, as though it had happened to someone else. Even in the early weeks after he returned home, unexpected movement nearby made him flinch as though he were back in danger, and he could not trust reassurance. Because he had come to believe the world was unsafe and that he could not trust his own judgment, almost anything could serve as a trigger: a boot on a trail, a uniform at work, a voice raised on the television, or someone moving too quickly in his peripheral vision. Each of those moments seemed to confirm the same bleak conclusion, and the more certain he became of that conclusion, the more sensitive he was to the next cue. Friends told him he was safe; his partner said the doors were locked; Arjun still scanned the room, convinced that safety could be taken away without warning. He also began to feel permanently humiliated by what had happened, certain that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, and the humiliation deepened his sense that he was set apart from everyone around him. Once he had reached those conclusions, almost anything could become a cue: a boot on a trail, a raised voice on the television, a stranger moving too quickly in his peripheral vision, even a uniform at work could suddenly seem significant and hold his attention. That humiliation made him more alert to possible signs that it could happen again; once he had decided he could not trust his own judgment, a raised voice, a stranger turning too quickly, or a uniform in the wrong place could all snag his attention and feel like proof that danger was nearby. Those appraisals quickly shaped how he moved through the world. Arjun came to believe that being seen carried risk, so he made himself smaller in public, avoided eye contact, and went along with whatever others wanted because agreeing felt safer than being noticed. He also imposed strict control over what he ate, cutting portions and skipping meals because regulating food gave him one area where he could feel disciplined and not at the mercy of anyone else. The same avoidance that seemed to protect him also narrowed his world into a map of things he could no longer tolerate; every route he stopped taking and every interaction he shortened became another reminder that danger was still running his days. If being seen felt risky and the safest thing was to keep himself small and predictable, then agreeing too quickly, avoiding eye contact, and skipping meals were not random habits for Arjun but the only responses that seemed to make sense. The memory would come back when he was trying to keep himself controlled, and after it surfaced he would tighten those routines further, telling himself that if he could just stay disciplined enough he might keep the images at bay. But the more he skipped meals and deferred to others, the more he felt that he needed those habits, and the more his life seemed to map itself around the captivity he was trying not to think about. At the same time, he found himself replaying scenes of revenge against the people responsible, imagining power reversed and himself no longer trapped. Those scenes were not just fantasies for him; they were what he turned to when the memory broke through, a way of keeping the event in view without feeling helpless inside it. The more those scenes stayed with him, the easier the captivity became to summon in his mind, and the more likely ordinary things — a closing metal gate at work, a boot scraping gravel on a trail, a sharp tone from a radio — were to feel linked to it. Even so, each time he returned to them, the captivity felt nearer and more dangerous, and he came away thinking that he must still be deeply changed by it. Yet these efforts never settled him for long. The more he tried to control his eating, please others, or mentally punish his captors, the more the images returned in sharper pieces, each flash of the event seeming to confirm how isolated and humiliated he had become. Each time the memory came back after he had been working so hard to keep it away, it seemed to tell him that he was not really in control of anything and that something about him had been permanently altered by what had happened. That constant sense of danger was itself part of the problem: when he felt most on edge, the snapshots came back with extra force, as if his body’s alarm were pulling him closer to the moment rather than away from it. On those days, the threat feeling did not stay abstract; it seemed to drag the memory forward whole, so that a sudden jolt on the trail or a burst of radio static could bring the fluorescent light, the metal door, and the grip on his arm back in one vivid rush. Feeling that threatened also made him more certain that the event had permanently altered him and that safety was something other people got, not him. The memory was especially liable to be pulled loose by military topics; if someone at home mentioned the army, or if a news report showed uniforms, his mind jumped straight back to those few terrible moments. Uniforms also set off the same reaction at work, where, as a park ranger, he sometimes encountered law enforcement or search-and-rescue personnel in similar clothing. Being seen in those moments felt exposing, and once he was self-conscious under someone’s gaze, he would think again that he had been foolish, weak, and uniquely unfortunate, which only made the old images more vivid and shameful. As the months passed, the memory itself started to drive the rest of the cycle. Keeping the memory at bay through strict routines and silence only seemed to keep it alive; the less he spoke about it and the more tightly he managed himself, the more intact and ready to return those snapshots felt. A sudden return of the snapshot images could bring a wave of bodily pain and make him feel as if the captivity were happening again, and once that threat feeling rose he became even more certain that he could not trust safety. When he was jolted by a sound or an abrupt movement on a trail, the room or forest seemed to tilt toward the past, and that sense of danger made the fragments of memory sharper still. The memories, in turn, fed back into his negative beliefs: each return seemed to prove that he remained isolated, permanently humiliated, and somehow at fault. Because he felt that way, he redoubled his efforts to keep control, eating even more strictly, deferring to others, and fantasizing about revenge in private. But these strategies brought their own costs. Skipping meals left him shaky and more reactive to sudden movement, which made the world feel even less safe. Going along with everyone else left him resentful and more aware of being unseen. Staying in those patterns without ever testing whether he could manage differently left the original threat feeling untouched, and in his body’s accounting that meant the danger must still be real. Revenge fantasies kept his mind circling the captivity long after work, making the images easier to summon and the humiliation harder to shake. And once he was already keyed up, even a uniform at the trailhead, a military comment on television, or a stranger turning too quickly on the path could trigger the same surge of dread and pull him back into the snapshots again. By the time he sought help, Arjun was still functioning at work but only by keeping himself tightly managed and on edge. His partner had noticed that he was distant at home, jumpy when someone moved unexpectedly, and increasingly unwilling to go out unless he could control the setting. What finally brought him in was the fear that he was becoming trapped in the same private loop every day: the images, the humiliation, the rigid control, the constant scanning. He said he was most afraid that the captivity had permanently changed him, but he was also hoping that therapy might help him feel safe enough to stop living as if danger were always one step away. After weeks of skipping meals and deferring to everyone else, he came to read those habits as proof that he could not manage on his own, which only deepened the humiliation and made him more certain that the event had changed him for good.
